water mains, sewers and other local improvements which are necessary to the building of new houses. For that reason, many municipalities do not encourage the building of new houses, and they very often forbid the construction of new houses in their localities.
In order to overcome this and many of the other difficulties which municipalities are encountering today, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) suggested a course of action while speaking in this house on November 24 last, as recorded at page 33 of Hansard. On that occasion he urged the federal government-	'
-to each agreement with the provincial governments in regard to a clearly defined re-allocation of taxing powers so that the provincial governments and municipal councils may have adequate financial resources to carry out their rapidly increasing responsibilities.
I believe that if this suggestion is followed by the government, the municipalities will be provided with sources of revenue from which they can finance the improvements which must be provided if new houses are to be built. I think it is obvious that we simply cannot build new houses unless the land is made available by the municipalities. Under present conditions municipalities have been reluctant, and as I have said, have often been completely unwilling to allow the building of new houses within their boundaries.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with the 20 per cent down payment which is now required on N.H.A. housing. The cheapest house that one can buy today through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation costs $10,000, which means that the prospective buyer must find $2,000 in cash before he can purchase a new house. In order to accumulate that $2,000, this man must earn at least $5,000 a year for at least four years. This means setting aside 10 per cent of his income for four years in a row, which I believe we will all agree is no mean feat.
For that reason I believe we will agree that a salary of $5,000 a year is the minimum on which this down payment can possibly be raised. I therefore believe that by following its present policy the government is rationing housing by the purse, and is making it virtually impossible for those with an income of less than $5,000 a year to buy a new house. After all, those are the people who need new housing most.
The government in the United States has taken a far more realistic attitude toward


this problem than has our government here. In the United States, the federal housing authority have set their down payment on a sliding scale, starting at 5 per cent, or $350 on a $7,000 house. When the value of the house is increased to $10,000, the down payment is increased to 12J per cent, or $1,250. This sensible policy which the United States government has adopted has made it possible for those with low incomes to buy new houses, and I believe that it is worthy of serious consideration by this government.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with a third obstacle in the way of those who want to buy new houses in Canada today. It is the 5| per cent interest charge on National Housing Act mortgages, and also the 20-year period within which those N.H.A. mortgages must be paid off. The combination of those factors puts the monthly carrying charges on a new house beyond the reach of a man with a modest income.
Once again, the United States government has taken a more practical view of this problem, and has made mortgages available at rates as low as 4 per cent. There, the regular amortization period is 25 years, and in many cases this period is extended to 30 years. These more generous terms have made it far easier for a man on a small income to buy a new house in the United States than is the case in Canada today. Once again, I believe that this policy merits serious consideration by this government.
In view of the far better housing effort in the United States owing to a more realistic housing policy, and in view of the fact that housing production in this country is falling farther behind demand every day, I believe there is no justification whatsoever for the obsolete and reactionary housing policy which this government is following. If the government persists in following its present policy, the present alarming housing shortage will continue to grow worse every day and families with four and five children will continue to live in one room for which they pay as high as $60 a month rent simply because they can find no other place in which to live.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that these conditions cannot be allowed to continue in a country which prides itself on having the highest standard of living in the world. I therefore urge this government to reconsider its housing policy in the light of three things; first, the present housing shortage which is increasing day by day; second the

ability of the construction industry to build far more houses than are being built at the present time, if given an opportunity; and third, the success which has been achieved in the United States, where practical housing policies have made housing available to the families which need it most.
As it is about one minute to six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and as I have considerably more to say, I would ask whether we could call it six o'clock.
The Budget-Mr. Hees
